content: 1. Receiving vaccines during pregnancy enables your body to produce protective antibodies, which can be transferred to your baby. These antibodies provide your baby with early protection against certain diseases during the first few months of life. 2. Vaccines such as flu, Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis), RSV (respiratory syncytial virus), and COVID-19 are safe for pregnant individuals and their babies. These vaccines have been thoroughly evaluated by experts to ensure their safety. While side effects may occur, they are generally mild, such as fever, fatigue, body aches, or localized redness and swelling at the injection site. 3. The Tdap vaccine is crucial during pregnancy to protect against whooping cough (pertussis), a potentially life-threatening condition for newborns. It is recommended to receive the Tdap vaccine between the 27th and 36th weeks of pregnancy, ideally earlier in this timeframe. Whooping cough can cause severe complications in infants, including difficulty breathing or even hospitalization. Adults and older children with mild symptoms can unknowingly transmit the disease to vulnerable newborns. 4. Receiving a flu vaccine during pregnancy is essential to protect both you and your baby. Pregnancy alters your immune, cardiovascular, and respiratory systems, increasing your risk of severe flu-related illness and complications. Fever during pregnancy, regardless of the cause, has been linked to adverse outcomes. The flu vaccine can also pass protective antibodies to your baby, safeguarding them during their first few months of life when they are too young to be vaccinated. 5. RSV is a common cause of severe respiratory illness in infants, potentially leading to difficulty breathing, feeding issues, and hospitalization. To protect your baby, you can either receive the RSV vaccine during weeks 32 to 36 of pregnancy (preferably between September and January) or opt for RSV immunization for your baby during their first RSV season if they are 8 months old or younger. 6. COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy is strongly recommended to protect both you and your baby from severe illness. Pregnant individuals are at higher risk of severe COVID-19 complications, which can also affect pregnancy outcomes. Evidence supports the safety and effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines during pregnancy, and vaccination can provide protection to babies under 6 months old, who are too young to be vaccinated themselves. 7. The timing of vaccinations during pregnancy is critical. For the flu vaccine, it is best to receive it in September or October, or earlier if you are in your third trimester during the summer months. The Tdap vaccine should be administered between weeks 27 and 36 of each pregnancy, preferably earlier in this window. The RSV vaccine is recommended during weeks 32 to 36 of pregnancy, and the COVID-19 vaccine can be received at any point during pregnancy. 8. It is important for anyone who will be in close contact with your baby to be up to date on all recommended vaccines. Newborns have underdeveloped immune systems, making them highly susceptible to infections. Parents, siblings, caregivers, and others should receive necessary vaccines at least two weeks before meeting the baby to allow time for antibody development. 9. If you become pregnant again, you will need to receive the Tdap vaccine during each pregnancy. Antibody levels from previous vaccinations decrease over time, and the protection provided during one pregnancy may not be sufficient for subsequent pregnancies. Additionally, you should receive a flu vaccine every flu season and stay current with COVID-19 vaccinations to ensure optimal protection for both you and your baby.
